holidays.name: National Hard Candy Day
holidays.description: A sweet-toothed celebration dedicated to lollipops, butterscotch discs, peppermint swirls, and every tooth-testing treat you can suck on, crunch, or heroically try not to bite. It's the perfect excuse to dig through grandma's candy dish and see what is lurking at the bottom.
holidays.origin: Like many American food days, it is an unofficial observance spread through candy lovers and calendar-keeping websites. It lands in the heart of the holiday season, when candy canes and ribbon candy fill homes and shops.
holidays.funFact: Hard candy is made by dissolving sugar in water and boiling it to the 'hard crack' stage, around 300 to 310 degrees Fahrenheit, so it turns into glass-like candy when cooled.

holidays.name: Look for an Evergreen Day
holidays.description: A nature-themed observance encouraging people to pause, step outside, and appreciate evergreen trees that stay green through the dreariest winter days. Bonus points for hugging a pine, though the sap may leave you with a sticky regret.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial, informal observance that grew out of the tradition of bringing evergreens indoors in winter. People have long used evergreens in midwinter festivals as symbols of life and endurance through the cold.
holidays.funFact: Not every evergreen is a conifer, and not every conifer is evergreen. Larch trees are conifers that turn golden and drop their needles each fall.

holidays.name: Oatmeal Muffin Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the humble, hearty oatmeal muffin, which sits somewhere between breakfast, snack, and dessert. Raisins are optional, though people argue about them with surprising passion.
holidays.origin: It is a food-lover's observance of the unofficial kind, popularized online in lists of national food days. Oats have been a breakfast staple for centuries, and muffins became wildly popular in America in the 19th century.
holidays.funFact: Oats were once considered a weed growing in wheat and barley fields before people realized they could be a crop in their own right.

holidays.name: Underdog Day
holidays.description: A day to cheer for the long shots, the little guys, and anyone nobody expected to win. It's a celebration of persistence, plucky heroes, and a certain cartoon dog in a cape.
holidays.origin: Underdog Day is tied to the pop culture legacy of the cartoon series 'Underdog,' a superhero cartoon about a humble shoeshine dog who speaks in rhyme. It's observed informally by fans of the show and by anyone who likes rooting for the underdog.
holidays.funFact: The cartoon 'Underdog' debuted in 1964, and its hero was a mild-mannered shoeshine boy named Shoeshine Boy who became Underdog by ducking into a phone booth, a classic superhero move.

holidays.name: Bill of Rights Day Adjacent: Doctor Who Appreciation Day Eve of Festive Specials
holidays.description: Fans of British pop culture often spend the days before Christmas gearing up for festive TV specials, snacks, and marathon viewing. It's a cozy, nerdy excuse to blanket-fort up with tea and your favorite show.
holidays.origin: There is no formal origin. It is a fan-created custom that grew from decades of British holiday television tradition, when networks reserved big special episodes for the Christmas season.
holidays.funFact: Christmas Day specials became a major tradition for British TV in the 1960s and 1970s, with millions of viewers tuning in at the same time.
